HOW TO READ THIS BOOK

One platform. Several kinds of truth.

A page can exist on the web, be fetched successfully, be present in an index, be relevant to a query and still be ineligible to appear. This playbook follows those transitions without treating them as the same event.

Documented behaviorOfficial product and protocol documentation describes observable rules. Citations identify the source and its scope.
Dated public researchPapers and public exhibits explain mechanisms at a stated time. They are not a complete current deployment map.
Proposed designThe fictional Atlas Search reference system connects the lessons into an implementable architecture with explicit assumptions.

Choose a reading path

Architecture first: Chapters 1-6, 17-23 and 53-62 cover state boundaries, publication and recovery.

Retrieval and ranking: Chapters 18-19, 24-38 and 63-64 connect lexical scoring, graph signals, semantic retrieval and evaluation.

AI Search: Chapters 9, 47-52 and 70 cover controls, evidence, scope and claim support.

Build and test: Chapters 65-72 and Appendices A-G provide sizing, operational cases, contracts and the local lab.

Read the evidence labels literally

Every chapter illustration is an original conceptual design unless its caption says otherwise. Charts are synthetic models or identified local experiments, not Google production telemetry. Proposed SLOs and costs are examples, not Google's private targets or commercial terms.

The dated source registry includes official documentation, Google research, standards, original retrieval research and public redacted exhibits. No leaked private repository or hidden exhibit text is treated as an authoritative current architecture.

Companion editions

The HTML offers offline search and enlarged diagrams. The PDF has linked contents and bookmarks. The source bundle contains editable material and local tests requiring no Google service.

PART 1 / Foundations and evidence
CHAPTER 01

Search is a continuously rebuilt view of the world

Start with the product contract, not a list of famous Google technologies.

What we are building

A search engine has to discover changing information, build representations of it, interpret a request, return useful evidence, and do all of this within a bounded time. It also has to remove information, respect publisher choices, resist manipulation, and explain operational failures. These obligations are related but not interchangeable. A fast answer can be wrong; an excellent ranking can contain a removed page; an available API can return an empty index.

Google publicly describes crawling, indexing and serving as distinct stages. Meeting its technical requirements does not guarantee that a page will be crawled, indexed or shown. Those are useful product boundaries, not a public map of its services. [S01] [S73]

Five planes in the proposed platform

The acquisition plane turns remote observations into versioned documents. The index plane builds lexical, vector, link and entity representations. The serving plane interprets queries and assembles results. The trust plane determines eligibility, removal and access. The learning plane evaluates outcomes and proposes better models. Trust must influence every other plane; it cannot be a nightly cleanup job.

A sixth, cross-cutting concern is economics: a crawl consumes someone else's server capacity as well as ours; a reranker consumes computation; an answer generator can multiply retrieval traffic. Every expensive step should have an explicit budget and a measurable contribution to usefulness.

Scope of this playbook

The core is public web Search. Images, video, local, news, commerce, Discover, ads, Knowledge Graph and AI experiences receive dedicated chapters because they change data contracts and serving behavior. Private connected context is treated as a separate authority domain. The book does not attempt to recreate every Google product, browser, advertising business or private codebase.

The reference implementation is called Atlas Search in worked examples. This is a fictional engineering design, not a Google system name. Its APIs, table names, operational targets and capacity estimates are proposals. Google system names appear only with source and time context.

The central mental model

Think of four independent questions: What did we observe? What did we publish? What is currently allowed? What did we show? A fetch receipt answers the first, a release manifest the second, a current policy decision the third, and a response trace the fourth. Joining these records lets an operator explain why a particular version appeared without pretending that a later crawl describes an earlier answer.

For example, a restaurant changes its opening hours at noon. A 10:00 crawl is not evidence of its 12:05 state. The engine can show the last observation with appropriate context, fetch a licensed current feed, or decline to make a confident real-time assertion. It must not silently transform historical evidence into current certainty.

First design decision

Build a narrow, high-quality corpus before a broad, weakly governed one. A first release can index approved technical documentation with exact retrieval and explicit source timestamps. The same contracts then extend to more languages, larger corpora and more complex ranking. Scaling a confused notion of document identity merely creates a larger debugging problem.

PART 1 / Foundations and evidence
CHAPTER 02

What public evidence can and cannot reveal

Read a 1998 paper as history, a 2025 exhibit as partial evidence, and a 2026 announcement as a dated product statement.

A layered evidence model

The 1998 Brin-Page paper documents an early Google prototype. The 2009 Dean talk describes information-retrieval infrastructure and earlier architectural choices. Neither is a complete inventory of the present system. Their enduring value is the problem structure: distributed acquisition, compact indexes, ranking signals and latency-sensitive retrieval. [S07] [S09]

We use four labels. Documented means a public source explicitly supports the statement. Historical research identifies its publication era. Proposed design means a mechanism developed here to build a comparable capability. Illustrative means a synthetic example or assumed workload. A diagram can be technically plausible and still be only a proposal.

A concise engineering timeline

Era Publicly described development Safe interpretation
1998 Early hypertext search architecture A prototype and its design tradeoffs
2003-2006 GFS, MapReduce, Bigtable Published infrastructure foundations
2010 Caffeine and Percolator A then-deployed incremental indexing transition
2018-2022 BERT and published neural-search explanations Learning augments language understanding and ranking
2025 Released redacted engineer-call notes Partial evidence about named ranking components
2026 AI Search and publisher-control announcements Dated behavior and rollout statements

The infrastructure and product sources for these eras are collected in the registry. Their coexistence in this table is not evidence that every component is on one current request path. [S08] [S12] [S30] [S40] [S54] [S55] [S58] [S80]

Public exhibits need careful handling

Two released redacted exhibits contain notes of engineer calls dated January 31 and February 18, 2025. They discuss signals and ranking terminology. This playbook uses only their visible public content, attributes the call dates, and does not infer the text hidden by redactions. Notes are not source code, a service dependency graph, or proof that every described mechanism is unchanged. [S10] [S11]

How to evaluate an architecture claim

Ask whether the source says the technology was researched, deployed in one product, deployed at a specific time, or used universally. These are different claims. A Cloud product built on an internal technology does not prove that Search stores a particular table in the corresponding public Cloud service. A patent describes possible inventions; by itself it is not deployment evidence. A leaked field name does not establish whether the field is active, significant or even on the main ranking path.

The useful engineering response is not to stop at uncertainty. Instead, define the required property, propose a mechanism, and test it. For example, we cannot infer the exact current publication protocol. We can still design a generation manifest that prevents half-built indexes from being served, and demonstrate its failure cases locally.

Reading rule

Every source-backed paragraph is intentionally bounded. Longer implementation discussions derive a reference system from requirements and tradeoffs. Treat all code, schemas, algorithms and unlabeled implementation choices as Atlas proposals, not recovered Google internals. The research cutoff is 27 September 2026; availability remains product-, country- and account-dependent where the sources say so.

PART 1 / Foundations and evidence
CHAPTER 03

Entities, versions and non-negotiable invariants

A URL, a document, a fetched version and a ranked result are four different objects.

The minimum logical model

A URL record describes a normalized address and its discovery history. A fetch receipt records one attempted observation, including time, status and validators. A document version binds extracted content to a successful receipt and parser version. A canonical cluster groups candidate representations without erasing their original addresses. An index generation identifies a compatible published set of representations. A policy record can override whether any of those representations are eligible now.

A query request carries text or multimodal inputs, locale, explicit filters, deadline and request identity. A candidate is a document or passage proposed by retrieval. A ranked result includes scores, provenance, eligibility decision and display metadata. An answer claim refers to supporting evidence spans, not merely a list of URLs.

Identity must survive change

Assign opaque document identifiers independently of storage location. Preserve URL aliases and redirect observations with validity intervals. Content hashes identify byte or normalized-content equivalence, but do not replace document identity: two independent publishers may publish identical text with different permissions and provenance.

Version every derived artifact. A posting references document version 18; an embedding also declares its model and tokenizer generation. A feature value records the observation and computation that produced it. The system can then reject a query vector from model B against document vectors from model A instead of silently returning meaningless neighbors.

Invariants to protect

Invariant Enforcement point
An obsolete crawl cannot overwrite a newer accepted observation Conditional write on observation version
A published release has complete, verified shard coverage Manifest validation before pointer update
Current removal overrides an old index or cache Serving-time policy barrier
Private evidence never enters a public result or shared cache Scope labels and authorization at joins
One logical event has at most one committed effect Transactional inbox/outbox and uniqueness
A result can be traced to the evidence actually served Response provenance record

These are proposed correctness properties, not a published Google schema. They are deliberately stronger and more testable than vague goals such as "eventually everything is consistent."

Observation time is not commit time

Keep observed_at, received_at, committed_at and published_at separately. A fetch started first can finish last. Wall-clock timestamps alone are poor conflict resolution when clocks drift or requests overlap. Use an owner-issued monotonically increasing observation sequence and a fencing token; record wall time for interpretation and operational diagnosis.

A policy revocation needs a separate monotonic epoch. A new content version does not automatically undo a legal removal, publisher opt-out or private access revocation. Restoration must be an authorized new policy decision, not a side effect of finding the same bytes again.

Design exercise

Suppose a crawler fetched version 7, a publisher requested removal, and an old worker later submitted a successful parse of version 7. The correct answer is not "last write wins." The parse may be retained as restricted evidence if permitted, but it cannot reset the removal epoch or make the document eligible. That separation is the foundation for the recovery mechanisms later in the book.

PART 1 / Foundations and evidence
CHAPTER 04

High-level architecture: acquisition is not serving

Keep slow, hostile and failure-prone work away from the interactive query path.

Proposed service boundaries

The acquisition side contains discovery, a frontier, per-origin scheduling, HTTP fetching, isolated rendering, extraction, canonicalization and durable document storage. It publishes accepted mutations through an outbox. Index builders consume those mutations, construct immutable segments, validate shard manifests and publish compatible generations.

The serving side contains edge admission, query understanding, a planner, lexical and semantic retrieval, feature lookup, reranking, eligibility enforcement, result composition and optional answer generation. It reads published indexes and current policy state. It does not block ordinary searches on a new crawl, a complete link-graph recomputation or a warehouse query.

A control plane handles configuration, model approval, publication, removal policy and ownership. A data plane handles requests against approved snapshots. Control-plane failure should not stop public queries against a known-good release, but it must not cause a serving cell to fabricate current authorization for private or withdrawn content.

Write ownership

Choose one authoritative writer per mutable key or use transactions with an equivalent conflict model. Frontier ownership can be partitioned by origin; document metadata by document ID; policy by authority scope. An index generation is an immutable artifact set plus a small mutable release pointer. A search result is mostly read-only computation and need not become a durable transaction unless it triggers an action.

Critical versus optional dependencies

Dependency On public query path? Failure behavior in the reference design
Published lexical index Yes Route to compatible replica or fail clearly
Current removal barrier Yes Enforce bounded freshness; exclude uncertain scope
Expensive neural reranker Optional by query class Use evaluated lexical/cheap-ranker fallback
Ads and optional vertical cards Independent Omit failed module; keep organic results
Answer generator Optional Return search results without generated answer
Analytics warehouse No Buffer minimal events; do not stall queries

An index is a serving artifact, not the database

A metadata database is excellent for a conditional document update but poor for intersecting millions of term postings under tight latency. A vector index is excellent for approximate similarity but cannot independently prove current access. A columnar warehouse is excellent for experiments but should not determine whether a fresh withdrawal is honored. Choose representations by access pattern and connect them through versioned contracts.

Deployment shape

Start with one region and several independent serving cells. Each cell holds a complete logical shard set for its assigned corpus, with replicas across failure domains. Acquisition and indexing capacity can scale separately. At larger scale, hierarchical brokers reduce fanout and admission controls keep background work from overwhelming shared storage.

This architecture deliberately does not name a guessed Google service for every box. Public descriptions establish product behavior; the dependency decomposition is an original build design. It is useful precisely because every boundary has an owner, a data contract, a deadline and a recovery plan.

PART 1 / Foundations and evidence
CHAPTER 05

Reliability means latency, usefulness and freshness

A 200 response is not enough to call a search successful.

Separate the indicators

An availability indicator counts eligible requests receiving a valid response. A latency indicator counts requests within a stated deadline. A completeness indicator checks shard coverage and required filters. A quality measure evaluates whether the response helps the user. Freshness measures the age of the evidence for a query class, not merely the timestamp of the latest deployment.

Google's SRE literature treats SLOs as targets tied to user experience and error-budget decisions. The targets below are our design examples; they are not Google's contractual Search SLA. [S68]

An illustrative starting contract

Capability Example internal target Important denominator
Public lexical search 99.95% valid responses over 28 days Admitted public requests, excluding explicit client cancellation
Interactive search latency 99% within 400 ms server-side Same request population; all supported locales
High-priority document update 95% visible within 10 minutes after accepted fetch Eligible, successfully parsed updates
Verified removal enforcement 99.9% within 60 seconds after policy commit Online eligible serving cells; breaches are incidents
Generated answer Separately measured completion and grounding Queries actually admitted to generation

These values require measurement and may be inappropriate for a particular product. For a 28-day time-based 99.95% target, the nominal unavailable allowance is 20.16 minutes. A request-based error budget is a count of bad requests, not automatically the same duration. A burst during peak usage consumes it differently.

Freshness has several clocks

User-visible age includes discovery delay, waiting for a crawl, transfer, rendering, extraction, indexing and publication. Instrument each segment. A fast indexing pipeline cannot compensate for a frontier that has not revisited a changed page for a month. Conversely, crawling every minute is wasteful when rendering queues take hours.

Define separate classes: immutable archives, ordinary reference pages, frequently changing inventory, event information and removals. Different classes deserve different effort and different uncertainty displays. Avoid a single global "freshness percentile" that hides stale safety-critical documents behind millions of unchanged pages.

Error budgets need a policy

When the query path burns its budget, stop experiments that increase fanout, reduce optional work, and prioritize the failing dependency. A correctness breach involving private leakage or ignored removal is not compensated by a large availability budget. These are guardrails with incident severity, not percentages to trade away casually.

Exercise the degraded modes

Inject a slow reranker, an unavailable ads module, an overloaded rendering pool and an expired policy cache separately. Expected behavior differs. Organic results can survive the first two. Rendering delay should show up in freshness metrics without slowing old-index reads. An expired private authorization cache must not be treated as permission.

The operational objective is an honest, bounded response: known corpus coverage, known release, enforced policy and explicit fallback. That contract is more meaningful than a dashboard that stays green while results silently disappear.

PART 1 / Foundations and evidence
CHAPTER 06

Two journeys: a changed page and a new query

Trace the asynchronous update path separately from the synchronous read path.

Journey A: a document changes

At 09:00 a publisher updates a page. The engine does not know this until it receives a trustworthy hint or observes the origin. A sitemap timestamp can prioritize work, but it is not proof of changed content. A crawler obtains an origin permit, fetches with available validators, records the response and releases its permit. A renderer may produce a second representation if necessary. Extraction then creates a new document version.

The mutation is committed with an outbox event. Consumers update lexical segments, vector work queues and derived features independently. A release validator verifies the required artifact set. Publication changes a small pointer from generation 41 to 42. Serving cells load 42, verify integrity and report readiness before receiving traffic for that generation.

Journey B: a user asks a question

The edge creates a request context and deadline. Query understanding determines language, possible entities and useful rewrites. The planner selects retrieval paths and budgets. Shard replicas return bounded candidate sets. The broker merges candidates, fetches features, reranks and filters against current policy. The composer creates titles, snippets and optional modules. A generated answer, when used, receives only approved evidence and must preserve its provenance.

A query normally runs against a published snapshot, not against the moving collection of all updates in progress. The policy overlay remains current enough to stop withdrawn content even when the snapshot predates the withdrawal.

The race worth understanding

Imagine query Q starts on generation 41. During its reranking step, a removal commits for document D. A robust contract specifies the final authorization point. In Atlas, the composer obtains a sufficiently current policy decision just before exposing D. For streaming answers, evidence that has not yet passed the barrier is not sent to the user. Material already sent cannot be unsent; the system therefore tracks exposure time and uses a short validity window for sensitive streams.

Observability joins the journeys

Record the request ID, normalized-query fingerprint, locale, release ID, retrieval-model ID, candidate origins, policy epoch and fallback reasons. Store raw query text only when permitted and for an appropriate retention period. On the acquisition side retain fetch sequence, parser version, document version and publication lineage. Operators should be able to join these without having broad access to private user context.

What an acceptance receipt means

A frontier enqueue receipt means work was recorded. A successful fetch means bytes were received. An index build receipt means artifacts exist. A publication acknowledgment means a release pointer committed. A query response means a representation was returned. None of these, by itself, means the page is globally current or the user found the answer useful.

This disciplined vocabulary prevents retry bugs. When a publication response is lost, reread the release pointer using the same operation identity. Do not generate a new release blindly. When a search response is lost, repeating a read is generally safe; repeating an associated booking action is a different operation requiring its own idempotency contract.

PART 2 / Discovering and understanding the web
CHAPTER 07

URL discovery and identity without destructive normalization

A crawler starts by deciding which addresses represent work, not by downloading everything it sees.

Sources of discovery

Accepted links, sitemaps, approved feeds, redirects and explicit publisher submissions all create discovery candidates. Store the source of each candidate: a URL found on an old spam page deserves different treatment from an update in a verified feed. Google describes sitemaps as a discovery aid rather than a crawl or indexing guarantee. Its 2023 announcement also deprecated the sitemap ping endpoint and emphasized meaningful modification timestamps. [S24] [S25]

A safe URL key

Parse the URL with a standards-aware library. Permit only supported schemes. Normalize host casing and well-defined default ports, remove the fragment for ordinary HTTP resource retrieval, and resolve relative links against the correct base URL. Preserve the original string and the normalized key. Reject malformed encodings, credentials in public crawl URLs, excessive length and unsupported address forms.

Do not alphabetically reorder query parameters or discard everything called id, ref or page by default. Some origins treat order, repetition or case as meaningful. Do not decode a reserved escaped slash into a path separator. Do not collapse HTTP and HTTPS, distinct ports or separate hostnames merely because they look similar. Aggressive normalization is a learned, origin-specific optimization that requires evidence and rollback.

A discovery record

A proposed record contains url_id, normalized URL, origin key, discovered-at time, referring document version, discovery method, crawl-class hint and dedup fingerprint. The origin key is the scheme/host/port authority used for robots and scheduling. DNS-resolved network targets are separate and can change.

Partition the discovery log by normalized URL hash, but partition scheduling state by origin. This avoids two independent frontier workers overwhelming the same website just because its URLs hash to different partitions. A stable URL identity also allows every rejection or deferral to be inspected later.

Infinite spaces need quotas

Calendars, faceted commerce filters, session identifiers and generated search pages can create effectively unbounded URL spaces. Maintain per-origin and per-pattern budgets, estimate marginal content novelty, and stop expanding a pattern that yields mostly duplicate or empty documents. Keep a small exploration budget so an early mistake does not permanently hide a useful section.

A Bloom filter can cheaply reject many already-seen candidates, but false positives must not become permanent loss of important discoveries. Confirm high-priority candidates against durable state, and periodically rotate or rebuild probabilistic filters. The authoritative URL table remains the source of scheduling truth.

Failure drill

A publisher moves from /guide?id=17 to /guide/17, while an unrelated page uses /guide?id=71. A careless normalizer dropping the query merges two documents. Test that keys remain distinct until redirect or canonical evidence establishes a relationship. Preserve aliases even after consolidation so removals, link signals and diagnostics refer to the correct historical address.

Operational question: can a publisher explain why an address was discovered but not scheduled? Store reason codes such as duplicate-pattern budget, robots deferral, origin overload or low expected value. A silent missing queue item is much harder to diagnose than an explicit decision.

PART 2 / Discovering and understanding the web
CHAPTER 08

The crawl frontier: spend effort where information changes

Scheduling is a constrained optimization problem with fairness, freshness and exploration.

Work is not a single FIFO

A first-in-first-out queue allows a huge low-value site to delay urgent changes elsewhere. Use a two-level frontier: a queue of eligible origins, each with a priority queue of URLs. Origin eligibility depends on politeness, recent errors and permits. Within an origin, prioritize expected information value, elapsed time, change likelihood and cost. Google's crawl-budget documentation distinguishes crawl capacity from crawl demand; that is a useful separation of constraints from value. [S17]

A reference priority function

For URL u, consider priority = expected_usefulness * change_probability * staleness_penalty / expected_cost. This is a design heuristic, not Google's formula. Include a minimum exploration term so new pages can be discovered. Use separate queues for verified removals, urgent updates, normal recrawls and exploratory discovery. Critical removals should not compete with arbitrary link expansion for the same global worker budget.

Estimate cost from historical response size, latency and rendering requirements. Estimate change probability from observations with censoring awareness: two identical crawls do not prove no changes happened between them. A page can change and revert. Features should reflect uncertainty rather than pretending the observation sequence is continuous monitoring.

Leases and fencing

When a worker receives a URL, issue a lease with origin_epoch, url_sequence, expires_at and a unique attempt ID. Permit renewal only by the current owner. A completion must match the accepted sequence before it can advance scheduling or content state. If the lease expires and another worker takes over, the original worker's late result cannot silently overwrite the newer one.

Do not make the lease itself the only proof of external concurrency. A timed-out request may still be running on a remote server. Keep conservative draining time or connection cancellation accounting before granting replacement origin capacity. Distributed ownership prevents duplicate local commitments; it does not magically stop bytes already sent over the network.

Fairness and starvation

Use weighted fair scheduling across origins and workload classes. A large site may receive more capacity but should not monopolize global renderer slots. Bound queue depth per tenant or verified publisher. Age waiting work gradually so a low-priority origin is not ignored forever, while hard safety exclusions remain hard.

Persist scheduling decisions and acknowledgments transactionally. A worker crash after recording a result but before acknowledging the queue should produce a harmless redelivery. A crash before recording it should allow retry. The consumer must distinguish these by attempt identity rather than by guessing from elapsed time.

What to measure

Track frontier age by class, time spent blocked on robots, origin permit utilization, novel documents per fetched byte, change yield, and work discarded because of obsolete leases. High fetch throughput with low useful-change yield is a warning, not a success metric. In a first deployment, simple deterministic priorities are often easier to debug than an opaque learned scheduler.

PreviousContentsNext chapter
PART 2 / Discovering and understanding the web
CHAPTER 09

Robots, noindex, preview controls and AI opt-outs

Separate permission to fetch from permission to index, preview or use content in a particular product.

The protocol boundary

RFC 9309 defines robots exclusion behavior, including selection of matching rules. It explicitly does not make robots rules an authorization mechanism. Google also notes that a disallowed URL can still appear through information from elsewhere, and that a crawler cannot observe a page's noindex directive when it is prevented from fetching the page. [S14] [S15]

Store robots policy by scheme, host and port, together with fetch time, response evidence and parser version. Interpret successful robots responses, unavailable resources and network failures according to the applicable protocol and documented crawler policy. Do not reuse the behavior of a page's 404 response as the behavior of a robots fetch failure. When policy is uncertain, defer rather than silently expanding access.

Controls answer different questions

Control Question answered Not equivalent to
Authentication / network access May this requester receive the resource? robots.txt
robots.txt May this crawler automatically fetch this path? Guaranteed index removal
noindex Should this fetched resource be excluded from indexing? Blocking the HTTP request
nosnippet / preview limits What excerpt or preview may be displayed? Removing the URL itself
Product-specific AI preference May content participate in a named AI use? A universal ban on all search uses

The preview directive vocabulary is documented separately from crawl control. Preserve its scope through extraction, snippets and answer evidence selection. [S20]

The important 2026 update

Google's June 2026 publisher announcement, updated August 31, says the dedicated Search Console control for generative-AI Search inclusion and associated insights had rolled out worldwide. It covers appearing in and grounding Search generative-AI features without being a ranking signal outside those features. This is distinct from Google-Extended, whose documented scope covers specified Gemini training and grounding uses and does not affect ordinary Search inclusion or ranking. [S80] [S76]

Do not repeat older advice that the only choice is to block all Googlebot access. Product controls evolve. An implementation should model named purpose grants rather than compressing every preference into a single crawl_allowed boolean.

Proposed enforcement model

Represent policy as a versioned vector: automatic-fetch permission, public-index eligibility, preview budget, generative-answer eligibility and retention constraints. Attach a policy snapshot to acquired content for provenance, but obtain a current decision at serving time. A cached snippet created under an older permission must not bypass a later restriction.

For publisher changes, commit the policy update before dispatching asynchronous index cleanup. Invalidate affected answer and snippet caches. For private resources, publisher hints are insufficient: verify the user's authority independently and never put their content in the public corpus.

Test the confusion cases

Test blocked crawling with an externally known URL, noindex on a fetchable page, a preview-only restriction, an AI-only opt-out, an expired robots cache and a change during answer streaming. The expected result differs for each. Store the reason and policy version used so support can diagnose the distinction without guessing.

PreviousContentsNext chapter
PART 2 / Discovering and understanding the web
CHAPTER 10

HTTP fetching as an untrusted network operation

Downloading a page is both an I/O problem and a security boundary.

A bounded fetch contract

A fetch request contains the normalized URL, accepted observation sequence, origin permit, redirect budget, byte budget, timeout and allowed network policy. The result contains status, headers, final address, redirect chain, validators, content hash, truncation flags and timing. A partial transfer must not masquerade as a complete document.

HTTP defines validators and conditional requests so a client can avoid transferring unchanged representations. A 304 response is meaningful only relative to a stored representation and the request's validator; it is not a fresh body. Status and method semantics come from HTTP, while indexing choices are a separate application policy. [S75]

Resolve, validate, connect, validate again

Use an egress proxy or equivalent network boundary that cannot reach internal metadata services, loopback, private address ranges or management networks. Validate every DNS result and every redirect target. Guard against DNS rebinding by connecting only to approved resolved addresses and checking the actual connection target. Limit response decompression as well as compressed bytes; a small archive or compressed page can expand enormously.

TLS verification, redirect handling and content-type sniffing should have explicit policies. Do not send credentials, cookies or user-specific headers in ordinary public crawling. Rendering subresources must use the same restricted network boundary, not a more privileged browser network stack.

Classify outcomes before retrying

An origin's 200 response can contain an error page. A transport timeout does not imply the document disappeared. A permanent redirect is evidence of address movement, but may still be temporary in the real world. Google documents distinct treatment of HTTP, DNS and network errors; transient failures can reduce crawling rather than establish immediate permanent deletion. [S22] [S23]

Use exponential backoff with jitter for retryable errors, an origin circuit breaker for repeated overload, and bounded attempts per observation. Track server-provided retry guidance where applicable. Avoid multiplying retries across proxy, fetcher and frontier: one logical attempt should have a known total budget.

Store evidence before interpretation

Write a durable fetch receipt even for a rejected or failed response. Large bodies go to object storage under content-addressed names; metadata references the object and integrity checksum. Commit the receipt before publishing a parse task. A parse worker must verify both integrity and accepted observation sequence before producing a new document version.

Do not preserve arbitrary hostile content indefinitely merely for debugging. Apply retention, quarantine and access controls. A sample of failure evidence can be enough if its purpose and privacy impact are understood.

Failure drill

A URL redirects from a public host to an internal IP after the first hop. The correct result is a blocked redirect with an auditable reason, not a fetched internal page. A second drill returns valid headers then stalls mid-body. The system should release resources, record a truncated attempt and reschedule according to policy, without indexing a misleading fragment as the authoritative complete page.

PreviousContentsNext chapter
PART 2 / Discovering and understanding the web
CHAPTER 11

Politeness, capacity and origin protection

The crawler should adapt to an origin, not behave like a distributed denial of service.

Two resources are being protected

The platform must protect its own sockets, workers and bandwidth. It must also avoid overwhelming remote websites. A global QPS limit is insufficient because thousands of workers can concentrate on one origin. A per-worker limit is insufficient because workers do not know one another's traffic. Coordinate permits per origin, with conservative shared-host controls where evidence shows a common bottleneck.

Google publishes crawler verification methods using IP ranges or forward-confirmed reverse DNS. A user-agent string alone is spoofable. The corresponding design lesson is to make your own crawler identifiable and provide a contact and abuse path; do not force publishers to guess which traffic is yours. [S81]

Reference admission algorithm

Maintain per-origin next_allowed_at, in-flight count, latency estimate, recent error rate and current owner epoch. A worker can begin only if time and concurrency conditions both pass. On a healthy completion, update observations and cautiously increase permitted rate. On overload signals or network failures, reduce concurrency and increase delay. Treat rendering subresource fetches as load too.

A token bucket smooths bursts, but a concurrency semaphore protects slow origins more directly. Use both where necessary. A website with a ten-second response time can be overwhelmed by a seemingly modest request rate if in-flight connections accumulate.

Shared infrastructure complicates limits

One IP can host many unrelated websites, and one origin can resolve to many IPs. Do not equate IP with publisher identity. Keep origin-level policy authoritative while using network-level overload signals as additional safeguards. Re-resolve DNS safely and expire network mappings; otherwise a CDN migration can inherit stale throttling indefinitely.

When an origin owner fails, fence future scheduling decisions. Existing requests may still be running, so replacement capacity should include a draining allowance. Absolute distributed remote concurrency is difficult to prove during failures; state the conservative bound and verify it in integration tests rather than claiming the lease makes it exact.

Backpressure across the pipeline

If render workers are saturated, reduce admission for render-heavy pages before object storage fills. If extraction is behind, fetch only high-value updates and retain bounded backlog. Queue length alone is misleading; estimated work in CPU-seconds, bytes and wall time better predicts recovery. Put disk and memory limits on every intermediate stage.

Operational dashboard

Track origin-level success and overload rates, effective in-flight requests, fetch latency, bytes, render fanout and age of deferred work. Alert on unexpectedly concentrated traffic and unexplained changes in response size. Provide a kill switch by origin and crawl class that propagates faster than ordinary scheduler configuration.

Acceptance test

Simulate a slow server with a rate-sensitive failure threshold. Add workers from one to one hundred. Throughput should stop growing at the configured origin budget rather than at the number of workers. Then kill the owner mid-request and verify that the replacement does not immediately issue a second full burst. This is a more realistic politeness test than checking a sleep call in one process.

PreviousContentsNext chapter
PART 2 / Discovering and understanding the web
CHAPTER 12

Rendering JavaScript without trusting the page

A browser is a powerful parser that executes an adversary-controlled program.

Why fetching is not always enough

Some pages contain useful content in initial HTML; others build it through JavaScript and remote resources. Google's documentation describes crawling, rendering and indexing as stages, with an evergreen Chromium-based renderer and restrictions around blocked resources. That establishes the need to reason about rendered representations; it does not reveal the private scheduler or sandbox implementation. [S18]

Proposed render job

Bind each job to an accepted fetch receipt, browser image version, viewport class, locale, resource policy and execution budget. The output includes a DOM snapshot, extracted text candidates, final URL, resource failures, console diagnostics and a completion reason. "Timed out after partial rendering" must be distinguishable from "successfully reached the chosen readiness criterion."

A document does not have one universal rendered state. It can depend on cookies, location, time, viewport and user actions. Public indexing should use explicit, reproducible contexts without inventing a logged-in user's view. Record context so changes in the browser image are not mistaken for changes in the publisher's content.

Sandbox architecture

Run renderers in disposable isolated workers with no cloud credentials, no internal network access, no shared writable profile and bounded filesystem use. Route subresources through the guarded fetch path. Disable unnecessary device capabilities and downloads. Separate sites and jobs strongly enough that one page cannot read another page's state or poison a shared cache with private data.

Timeouts need several dimensions: CPU time, wall time, memory, number of network requests, total decompressed bytes and DOM size. A page can remain busy forever through timers or streaming connections, so "network idle" is not a universal completion condition. Choose a bounded readiness heuristic and record when it is only approximate.

Reuse without incorrect equivalence

Cache immutable script and style resources by their actual content identity and HTTP semantics. Do not assume a filename ending in .js is immutable. A render cache key must include the input representation, browser version, context and relevant policy. Reusing yesterday's rendered DOM after a publisher removes a section can keep stale evidence alive.

Rendering every page is expensive. Start with HTML extraction, classify whether useful content is missing, and prioritize rendering when the expected gain justifies its cost. Keep a sample of apparently simple pages in the render path to detect classification mistakes. This is a proposed scheduling optimization, not a statement of Google's exact policy.

Failure drill

A page displays "in stock" only after an API request, but that API is blocked or unavailable to the crawler. The engine should not infer inventory from a hidden script template. Preserve the incomplete-render signal and avoid confident stock claims. Another page continuously appends nodes; the renderer must terminate within budget and quarantine the pathological job without taking down neighboring work.

PreviousContentsNext chapter
PART 2 / Discovering and understanding the web
CHAPTER 13

Extraction, document structure and multilingual text

The parser must preserve meaning and provenance before any ranking model can use them.

From bytes to a document

Extraction produces a structured representation, not just a bag of words. Preserve title candidates, headings, body sections, lists, tables, outgoing links, image references, language spans and publisher directives. Every text span should retain a mapping to its source document version and location. That mapping later supports snippets, passage ranking and grounded answers.

For PDFs and other supported formats, use format-specific parsers in isolated workers with size and complexity limits. A parser failure should not create an empty replacement for a previously valid document. Store the failure and keep or withdraw the prior version according to an explicit freshness and safety policy.

Text processing choices

Normalize Unicode carefully, detect script and language, and tokenize with a versioned analyzer. Case folding can help matching but destroy distinctions in some identifiers. Accent folding can improve recall but merge distinct words. Stemming can help one language and damage another. Keep the original text for display and evidence, plus normalized fields for retrieval.

Retain positions across removed stop words so a phrase does not falsely bridge a gap. Field boundaries matter: a word in a navigation menu is not necessarily the topic of the main article. A query for an exact product code should have a retrieval route that does not stem, split or translate away the identifier.

Language and locale are separate

A page can be written in English while targeting a particular region. Hreflang describes alternate language or regional versions; Google's documentation says it does not use hreflang or the HTML language attribute as the sole mechanism for detecting the page's language. Preserve alternate relationships instead of collapsing every translation into one text representation. [S77]

A proposed index can retain a language distribution over spans, a dominant-language label and regional applicability. Query understanding chooses compatible analyzers and may search across languages when explicitly useful. Cross-language retrieval should not silently replace an exact local regulation or product variant with a similar page from another jurisdiction.

Boilerplate and structured facts

Learn recurring page-template regions per site, but do not delete them blindly. A footer may contain the only contact address; a repeated table header supplies units. Separate low-weight boilerplate fields from main content rather than irreversibly stripping all repeated text.

Structured data is a claim by the publisher. Parse it, validate syntax and compare it with visible content. Google's structured-data guidance describes machine-readable markup for understanding and feature eligibility, not guaranteed appearance or independent verification of the facts. [S46]

Validation and observability

Measure extraction coverage, language confidence, malformed-encoding rates, text-to-source mapping integrity and differences between HTML and rendered output. Sample documents after every parser release. A change that suddenly halves average document length may be a parser regression rather than an improvement in boilerplate removal.

The key invariant is reproducibility: given the stored input, parser image, analyzer version and context, an engineer should be able to explain how the searchable representation was created. Without that, ranking regressions become impossible to separate from content-processing regressions.

PreviousContentsNext chapter
PART 2 / Discovering and understanding the web
CHAPTER 14

Duplicates and canonicalization without losing authority

Similarity reduces redundant work; it does not grant permission to merge unrelated publishers.

Three distinct problems

Exact byte duplicates can be detected with a cryptographic content hash. Near-duplicates require a similarity representation. Canonicalization chooses a representative among related URLs for a particular purpose. These are connected but different decisions. Identical text can be legitimately hosted by different organizations with different rights, freshness and authority.

Google documents redirects, canonical annotations and sitemaps as signals of differing strength for consolidation, while retaining its own canonical choice. The 2007 near-duplicate crawling paper studies SimHash-style detection. Neither establishes a universal present-day threshold or a rule that similarity alone determines canonical identity. [S19] [S13]

A proposed clustering pipeline

First create candidates with exact hashes and inexpensive locality-sensitive signatures. Then compare content, structure, link relationships, redirects and publisher hints. Store edges with confidence and evidence rather than immediately deleting all but one node. A cluster version chooses a representative while preserving aliases and per-member policy.

Avoid transitive over-merging: A is similar to B and B to C does not prove A and C are the same document. Large clusters deserve additional checks. A generic template or syndicated paragraph can connect otherwise unrelated pages. Use main-content evidence, provenance and maximum-cluster safeguards.

Canonical choice is contextual

For public web results, prefer a stable, eligible representative with strong supporting evidence. For a local-language query, another legitimate alternate may be more appropriate. For an exact URL lookup, the original address may still matter. Keep canonical identity separate from the presentation URL selected for a request.

A member-level removal must not be undone because another cluster member remains visible. Conversely, removing one URL does not automatically authorize removal of every similar document owned by other publishers. Model the scope of each decision explicitly: URL, document, cluster, site, geographic region or product purpose.

Changes and split operations

Canonical clusters evolve. A formerly duplicate page may become a distinct product. Use versioned membership and reversible merge operations. A split should restore member histories, link evidence and policy without inventing new unrelated identities. Derived indexes must know which cluster version supplied their representative mapping.

Redirect cycles and chains need bounded traversal. Record each observed edge and time; do not follow endlessly or assume a temporary redirect is a permanent identity change. A canonical hint to a blocked or unavailable target should not erase the source before the target is evaluated.

Failure drill

Two vendors copy the same manufacturer's description but have different prices, regions and stock. A text-only deduplicator merges them, then displays one vendor's price with the other's link. Prevent this by retaining structured offer identity and publisher provenance. Similarity is an optimization signal, not a license to combine facts from different commercial entities.

Design takeaway: deduplication should save bandwidth, computation and result-page space while leaving enough lineage to reverse an incorrect merge. An irreversible "duplicate=true" flag is too weak for a production search corpus.

PreviousContentsNext chapter
PART 2 / Discovering and understanding the web
CHAPTER 15

Recrawl scheduling and the mathematics of freshness

Freshness is a distribution of uncertainty, not a promise that the web has been observed continuously.

A useful simple model

Assume a page changes according to a Poisson process with rate lambda and is recrawled exactly every T time units. Under that deliberately simplified model, the probability it has changed t units after a crawl is 1 - exp(-lambda*t). Average freshness over the interval is (1 - exp(-lambda*T))/(lambda*T). This measures whether no change has occurred since the last observation, not whether the page reverted or the change mattered.

The model explains why the same schedule should not be applied everywhere. A frequently changing page benefits more from short intervals, but the benefit must be weighted by user demand, importance and fetch cost. A large low-value page changing every second can consume all capacity without improving meaningful results.

Learn from censored observations

The crawler sees snapshots, not a change log. If two snapshots differ, at least one change happened. If they match, changes may still have happened and reverted. Use conservative estimates, confidence intervals and publisher hints. Avoid treating an unreliable lastmod or Last-Modified timestamp as ground truth.

For a first system, use a small set of crawl classes with deterministic schedules and bounded adaptive adjustments. A complex learned scheduler is valuable only if its allocation decisions can be evaluated against a baseline. Reserve capacity for new sites and unexpected events so historical demand does not permanently lock in incumbents.

Separate recrawl from republication

A 304 response can refresh an observation without producing new postings. A changed body may require new text and embeddings but not a complete link-graph rebuild. A policy change may require immediate serving suppression without any new content fetch. Route mutations according to what changed, and preserve the dependency graph.

Maintain a freshness vector for each document: source observation age, extraction age, lexical-index age, embedding age and policy age. A response can then choose lexical retrieval when an embedding is too old, rather than discarding a fresh page entirely. Feature freshness contracts should be explicit per use case.

Queueing limits the result

Total visibility delay is discovery wait plus scheduling wait plus fetch/render time plus index processing plus publication lag. Measure both median and tail. When one component dominates, optimizing another is mostly cosmetic. A queue accumulating ten hours of render work cannot meet a ten-minute update objective regardless of how fast a single render runs.

Failure drill

An event causes a thousand pages to change at once. The scheduler should promote a bounded urgent class without starving verified removals or overloading origins. If capacity is insufficient, expose the backlog and prioritize information value; do not label all fetched-but-unpublished content "fresh."

The chart accompanying the capacity section uses the simple model above to show how freshness changes with the product lambda*T. It is a synthetic planning model, not a measurement of Google's recrawl schedule or a guarantee about any website.

PreviousContentsNext chapter
PART 2 / Discovering and understanding the web
CHAPTER 16

Deletion, withdrawal and the fast policy overlay

A removal must outrun slow index rebuilds and stale caches.

Removal is a state machine

Represent a removal request with authenticated authority, scope, reason, submitted evidence, review status, effective time and policy epoch. Scope may be a URL, a publisher-owned site, a region, a preview surface or a named AI use. Verification, review and enforcement are distinct stages. A support ticket is not itself an authorization to erase someone else's content.

Google documents noindex as a fetched directive for index exclusion. Search Console's public inspection vocabulary also distinguishes observed indexing and fetch states. These are publisher-visible semantics, not a disclosed internal database layout. [S21] [S74]

Proposed two-speed architecture

The fast path commits a policy change and distributes a compact exclusion overlay to serving cells. The slow path removes postings, vectors, snippets and derived evidence from future generations and retained stores according to policy. The fast path protects users while the slow path restores storage and index hygiene.

A serving cell advertises the minimum policy epoch it has applied. Routing refuses sensitive traffic to a cell below the required barrier. For ordinary public removal, define a measured propagation objective and alert on stale cells. For private authorization, use a stronger request-specific freshness condition rather than assuming a periodic broadcast is sufficient.

Prevent resurrection

A restored backup may predate the removal. Before rejoining traffic, the cell must replay the authoritative policy log or load a verified current snapshot. A delayed document update must not clear a tombstone. An old index release can be reused only with the current overlay, not with the policy state that existed when it was built.

Tombstones require retention long enough to cover replay, backup restoration and offline consumers. Deleting them too early can allow an ancient event to recreate removed data. Compaction should preserve the latest effective policy and the minimum sequence needed to reject stale mutations.

Cached and generated outputs

Invalidate query-result, snippet and answer caches by dependency. Each cached answer should identify the document versions and policy scope it used. A cache that stores only rendered HTML cannot reliably answer which withdrawal affects it. Dependency lists may be approximate for broad invalidation, but false negatives are unacceptable for required suppression.

Generated text complicates the problem because it may paraphrase evidence rather than quote it. Record claim-to-evidence lineage and prohibit unsupported reuse after the evidence becomes ineligible. This is a proposed safety property; exact legal retention and removal obligations require product-specific review.

Reinstatement is explicit

A successful appeal or publisher change creates a new authorized policy transition. It does not erase the history. Reindexing may require a new fetch if the old bytes are no longer current. Keep the audit trail separate from public serving data and limit access to sensitive reasons.

Failure drill

Publish generation 12, remove document D at epoch 19, then restore generation 10 and replay D's old update. D must remain suppressed. Test the same sequence with an answer cache and a vector-only candidate path. A deletion design that protects only lexical postings is incomplete.

PreviousContentsNext chapter
PART 3 / Building searchable indexes
CHAPTER 17

The index family: one corpus, many access paths

A search engine stores several purpose-built representations of the same versioned evidence.

Different access paths need different representations

Term lookup needs document IDs; phrase queries need positions; snippets need source offsets; vector retrieval needs embedding structures. Link analysis and current policy have different access patterns. One physical record layout cannot efficiently serve every path.

Atlas separates its document evidence store from lexical, passage, vector, graph, feature and policy representations. Each has a freshness and compatibility contract. Retain the metadata required to reproduce every rebuildable derivative.

A segment is an immutable unit

An index segment contains a term dictionary, postings blocks, document metadata, field statistics, optional stored fields, deletion references and checksums. It declares analyzer version, document-version range, schema version and build identity. Immutable segments are easy to replicate and validate. Updates create new segments and mark old document versions obsolete.

A generation manifest lists exactly which segments and auxiliary tables form a searchable release. It also identifies corpus statistics and compatible query analyzers. A query chooses a generation at admission and keeps it through retrieval and ranking unless a documented transition protocol says otherwise.

Publication versus freshness

Not every auxiliary feature must be rebuilt at the same cadence. A link score may be older than text postings, while a removal policy must be newer. The manifest therefore includes compatibility ranges and feature timestamps, not an unrealistic assertion that every fact was computed simultaneously. The ranker knows how to handle missing or stale optional features.

Proposed ownership matrix

Representation Key Typical update pattern
Document evidence Document ID + version Append immutable version
Lexical postings Field + term + segment Build and merge
Vector index Model generation + vector ID Batch or incremental insertion
Link graph Source version + target identity Edge delta and periodic compaction
Feature table Entity + feature definition version Versioned upsert
Policy overlay Authority scope + epoch Strongly ordered mutation

Rebuildability is a product feature

Keep enough input lineage to rebuild an index after a parser or analyzer bug. Rebuilding from live websites alone is not reproducible because the source may have changed or disappeared. Retention and privacy constraints may limit what can be kept; when evidence cannot be retained, record that limitation and design a recrawl-based recovery path.

Failure drill

A new tokenizer splits product identifiers differently. Text postings are rebuilt, but the query analyzer remains old. Requests return fewer exact matches without obvious errors. Prevent this by validating analyzer compatibility during release publication and including exact-identifier fixtures in the canary corpus. A green storage checksum does not prove semantic compatibility.

PreviousContentsNext chapter
PART 3 / Building searchable indexes
CHAPTER 18

Inverted indexes, positions and field-aware retrieval

Turn the question "which documents contain this term?" into a direct lookup.

A tiny worked corpus

Use three original example documents: D1 = "red fox runs", D2 = "blue fox sleeps", D3 = "red bird flies". The term fox has postings for D1 and D2; red has postings for D1 and D3. Their intersection returns D1. The positional posting for fox in D1 is position 1 when counting from zero. A phrase query for "red fox" checks adjacent positions, not merely both words somewhere in the document.

This is standard information-retrieval background; the examples and implementation choices here are original. [S79]

What a posting contains

At minimum store document ID and term frequency. For phrases and proximity, store positions. For field-aware ranking, separate title, heading, body and anchor-text fields or tag occurrences by field. A posting may reference a compact document ordinal within a segment, which maps to stable document ID and version in a side table.

Do not confuse document frequency with term frequency. Document frequency counts how many documents contain a term. Term frequency counts occurrences in one document. Corpus size and average field length are additional statistics used by scoring functions. Statistics need a declared scope: segment, shard or whole generation.

Query execution basics

For an AND query, start with the shortest posting list and intersect using ordered advances. For an OR query, merge candidate IDs and accumulate contributions. Phrase verification can be deferred until cheaper filters reduce the candidate set. Exact quoted phrases should preserve analyzer semantics, including stop-word gaps and punctuation choices documented by the product.

A very common term can have a huge posting list. Avoid loading it all into memory. Decode blocks on demand, use skip metadata, and stop according to a proven top-k condition or a declared approximation budget. The next chapters explain how compression and safe upper bounds make this efficient.

Document updates and duplicates

If D1 version 2 replaces version 1, both may temporarily exist in immutable segments. A generation-level live-document map determines which version is eligible. Without this map, the same logical page can appear twice or contribute twice to corpus statistics. Segment compaction eventually removes obsolete versions, but correctness must not depend on compaction finishing first.

Anchors and provenance

Anchor text can describe a target using words absent from its body. Store the source document version and target mapping so spam controls and later canonical changes can be applied. Do not blindly add every incoming anchor to the target's body field; that destroys provenance and makes poisoning difficult to diagnose.

Implementation exercise

Build a positional index for ten documents. Verify AND, OR, exact phrase and field-restricted queries. Then replace one document and ensure the old version cannot match. Inspect the posting lists directly. Understanding these few structures is more valuable than memorizing a diagram with an unexplained "search database" box.

PreviousContentsNext chapter
PART 3 / Building searchable indexes
CHAPTER 19

Compression, skips and memory locality

The fastest byte is often the one the query does not have to fetch or decode.

Why sorted IDs compress well

Posting lists are ordered by document ordinal. Instead of storing IDs 100, 104, 109 and 110 directly, store a base and gaps 4, 5 and 1. Small nonnegative integers can use variable-length or block-packed encodings. Positions can be delta-encoded within a document as well. This is an original small example of standard index-compression reasoning, not a description of Google's current codec.

Compression saves storage and network bandwidth but consumes CPU to decode. The best format depends on list length, access pattern, SIMD support and how often queries skip blocks. Choose a few well-tested codecs rather than an unbounded set of special cases that make corruption recovery and upgrades difficult.

Block metadata

For each block, store its last document ID, byte offset, document count and safe score-bound metadata when the scoring model permits it. A query can advance directly to a relevant block without decoding all earlier postings. Separate frequently accessed block headers from cold position streams so a simple term query does not read phrase data it never uses.

Checksums should cover both headers and payloads. A corrupted last-ID field can cause a query to skip valid matches even when the payload checksum would have passed had it been read. Validate monotonicity, lengths and boundary conditions during build and load.

Memory hierarchy shapes the layout

Keep hot dictionaries and small metadata in memory. Use memory-mapped or explicit buffered reads for larger posting blocks according to the operating environment. Measure page faults, decompression CPU and cache misses, not just bytes on disk. A smaller representation that triggers random reads can be slower than a somewhat larger sequential layout.

Document ordering affects both compression and locality. Grouping related documents may improve compression and query access, but can concentrate popular terms or sites into hotspots. Stable external document IDs should remain independent of internal ordinals so the layout can be changed during compaction.

Updates complicate statistics

A block's upper bound must remain safe for all live documents it covers. If a boost, length normalization or feature range changes after build, old bound metadata may no longer be valid. Publish compatible score definitions and bounds together. Otherwise a performance optimization can silently turn into a relevance bug.

Build and query tests

Test empty lists, one-element lists, maximum IDs, large gaps, repeated positions, corrupted lengths and truncated blocks. Verify that skipping and full decoding return the same candidate sequence. Fuzz decoders as untrusted binary parsers even though the builder is internal; disk corruption and software bugs are sufficient threats.

Tradeoff to remember

Do not optimize only compression ratio. The useful objective is end-to-end cost per correctly answered query under the expected workload. Include build time, merge amplification, replication traffic, warmup time and incident diagnosability. A slightly larger, simpler format may be the right first production choice when it allows safe rollouts and reliable recovery.

PreviousContentsNext chapter
PART 3 / Building searchable indexes
CHAPTER 20

Distributed index construction and compaction

Build large indexes as restartable transformations with deterministic identities.

The batch construction pattern

Read accepted document versions, tokenize fields, emit (field, term, document, positions) records, partition by the chosen index layout, sort and merge into posting lists. Google's MapReduce paper describes a general model for distributed map and reduce computations; the pipeline here is a reference application of those ideas, not a claim that every current Search index is built by that original system. [S55]

The builder must read a defined input snapshot or a bounded mutation interval. "Whatever is in the database while the job runs" produces inconsistent statistics and difficult-to-reproduce outputs. Record input manifest, parser/analyzer versions, job configuration and checksums.

Deterministic work units

Assign each task a content-derived or generation-scoped identity. A retry writes to a temporary artifact path, verifies output, then atomically registers the artifact. Two attempts must not both append duplicate postings to a shared final file. Speculative execution is safe only when finalization selects one equivalent result or detects a mismatch.

Partition skew matters. A very common term or large document can overwhelm one reducer. Use secondary partitioning, bounded per-document work and special handling for oversized records. Track bytes and CPU by partition before committing to a layout that looks balanced only by record count.

Compaction is not publication

Incremental updates create many small segments. Compaction merges compatible segments, removes obsolete versions and rebuilds local metadata. It can reduce query fanout and storage overhead, but it also consumes I/O and temporary space. Throttle compaction against serving needs and maintain enough free space for the worst concurrent merge plan.

A compacted segment is not visible merely because its file exists. It becomes visible when a validated generation manifest references it. Old segments remain available until all readers of the old generation have drained and retention rules allow deletion.

Watermarks and missed updates

Suppose a snapshot build covers mutations through sequence 1,000,000. Updates after that point belong to a delta stream. The release needs either a consistent snapshot plus catch-up deltas or a declared cutoff that serving understands. A gap between snapshot extraction and stream subscription can permanently lose documents. Record the handoff watermark transactionally.

Late events should be compared by document version and policy epoch, not ingestion time. Replaying an old mutation after compaction must not resurrect an obsolete or removed document. Keep the live-version map and tombstone logic in the replay path.

Failure drill

Kill a worker after it writes its output but before it reports success. Retry the task and verify a single registered artifact. Then corrupt one partition checksum and confirm publication is blocked even though all task counters say "complete." Job completion is a control-plane claim; artifact integrity and corpus coverage are the actual release conditions.

PreviousContentsNext chapter
PART 3 / Building searchable indexes
CHAPTER 21

Incremental indexing: the Caffeine and Percolator lesson

Update the affected pieces without pretending the entire corpus changes atomically.

What the historical sources establish

Google's 2010 Caffeine announcement described continuously processing small portions of the web rather than waiting for large layered refreshes. The Percolator paper described distributed transactions and notifications for incremental processing, including its then-deployed use in Google's web indexing system. These are dated accounts, not proof of the exact current update machinery. [S12] [S08]

Build a dependency graph

A changed document can affect its postings, outgoing links, canonical cluster, embeddings, snippets and derived features. Model those dependencies explicitly. Some transformations are cheap and synchronous with metadata acceptance; others are expensive and asynchronous. A change to one paragraph should not require rerendering every page that links to it.

Store a durable mutation record containing document ID, old and new versions, changed-field mask, policy epoch and event ID. Commit it with the accepted metadata update through a transactional outbox. Consumers maintain their own progress and deduplication records. Delivery may repeat; committed effects must not.

Transaction scope is a design choice

A database transaction can atomically accept a document version and its outbox event. It cannot cheaply atomically rebuild all lexical shards, vectors and link scores across the planet. Use local atomicity for authority and explicit eventual propagation for derivatives. The generation manifest declares which derivative versions are ready to serve together.

For a fast text update, publish lexical deltas while an embedding job is pending. The ranker can use a known fallback for the new version. It must not combine old semantic features with new text as though they were generated together when the feature contract forbids that combination.

Notifications are hints to inspect state

A notification should lead a worker to the latest authoritative document version. It should not force the worker to trust the event payload forever. If versions 8, 9 and 10 arrive before processing begins, the worker may coalesce compatible work to version 10 while retaining audit lineage. A removal event must retain its stronger semantics rather than being accidentally coalesced away by a later content update.

Hot documents and amplification

Frequently edited pages can produce more derivative work than the system can finish. Use debounce windows for nonurgent features, cancel superseded jobs where safe, and bound queued versions per document. Measure amplification as derived tasks and bytes per accepted source change. High amplification can consume more resources than the original crawl.

Failure drill

The metadata commit succeeds, but the queue publish fails. The outbox relay must eventually deliver the mutation. Then deliver the same event twice and an older version afterward. The current document should remain correct, and each derivative should converge without duplicated contributions. This is the practical value of explicit version ownership, not an assertion of exactly-once networking.

PreviousContentsNext chapter
PART 3 / Building searchable indexes
CHAPTER 22

Atomic generation publication and safe rollback

Never make half an index visible because a deployment counter reached 100%.

The release object

An Atlas generation manifest contains generation ID, parent generation, corpus cutoff, shard map, segment hashes, document-statistics version, analyzer version, compatible model IDs and minimum policy requirements. Sign or authenticate the manifest and store it immutably. Publication changes one small authoritative release pointer with compare-and-swap against the expected parent.

A build coordinator can fail at any point. The manifest must be independently verifiable so a replacement coordinator can determine whether publication happened. A lost acknowledgment is resolved by reading the pointer and operation record, not by creating a new generation with different contents under the same name.

Readiness is a semantic gate

Each serving replica downloads artifacts, validates checksums, loads indexes, checks compatibility and executes a canary query suite. Only then does it advertise readiness for that generation. Process health alone is insufficient: a worker can be alive with missing shards or an incompatible tokenizer.

For each request, the broker selects replicas that serve the same compatible generation. Mixing arbitrary shards from generations 41 and 42 can double-count moved documents or omit them entirely. A carefully designed rolling protocol can permit compatible mixes, but compatibility must be explicit rather than assumed.

Publication state machine

Use BUILT -> VERIFIED -> STAGED -> ACTIVE -> DRAINING -> RETIRED. Failed verification leaves an artifact quarantined. Activation requires sufficient ready capacity, not necessarily every machine. Draining waits for readers and rollback retention. Retirement deletes artifacts only after no active release or reader lease references them.

Reader leases need bounded duration and renewal. A crashed query should not pin old storage forever. Conversely, a long-running analysis job cannot silently lose its snapshot because the ordinary interactive-query lease expired. Different readers need different lifecycle contracts.

Rollback does not roll back policy

Switching from generation 42 to 41 can restore known-good retrieval behavior. It must not restore old removals, permissions or publisher preferences. Current policy remains a separate barrier. Optional feature tables also need compatibility checks: an old index with a new ranker may be as broken as the release being rolled back.

Migration across shard maps

When repartitioning, prepare the new map and complete data coverage before switching. Queries must know which map they use. A stable external document ID allows internal ordinals and shard locations to change. Keep both maps during a bounded drain period, and test that cross-shard deduplication does not hide a missing partition.

Failure drill

Two coordinators both try to publish children of generation 41. Exactly one compare-and-swap wins. The loser may rebuild or explicitly publish atop the new parent, but cannot overwrite the winner by retrying a blind assignment. Then simulate a committed activation with a lost response; the retry must return the same result. The local teaching model demonstrates this control-plane property without claiming distributed consensus implementation.

PreviousContentsNext chapter
PART 3 / Building searchable indexes
CHAPTER 23

Document partitioning, replicas and hierarchical fanout

Choose a partitioning scheme around the query work and failure domains, not just storage balance.

Document versus term partitioning

With document partitioning, each shard stores a subset of documents and their terms. A general query fans out to many shards, each returns local candidates, and a broker merges them. With term partitioning, postings for different terms live on different workers, reducing some fanout but creating expensive intersections and skew for common terms. Dean's 2009 talk discusses these historical tradeoffs; the present architecture below is our proposal. [S09]

Why document shards are a useful starting point

They make each shard a miniature search engine, simplify document-level policy and allow independent replication. Hash partitioning balances document counts reasonably, but not necessarily query CPU, posting volume or popularity. Range or topic partitioning can improve locality while creating skew and routing complexity. Measure the workload before choosing a more elaborate layout.

Each logical shard has replicas across independent failure domains. Replica selection considers generation compatibility, health, queueing and locality. A stale replica with low latency is not an acceptable substitute if it lacks required policy or schema state.

Hierarchical brokers

A root broker can delegate groups of shards to intermediate aggregators. Each level applies deadlines and returns a bounded candidate set. This reduces connection pressure but introduces a risk: an intermediate top-k cutoff can discard documents needed by a later global reranker. Candidate budgets must be justified for the scoring stage, with measured recall against a larger baseline.
